newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus backs Lukashenko, foes say vote was farce.
newsitem.headline: Belarus backs Lukashenko, foes say vote was farce.

text.p: Hardline President Alexander Lukashenko claimed a huge victory over parliament, the opposition and the highest court in Belarus on Monday after millions of voters gave him a mandate to assume sweeping powers.

"It will be very hard for my opponents to insist there were violations, that the referendum was illegal. The overwhelming majorities won by all the president's questions speak for themselves," a confident Lukashenko told a news conference.

More than 70 percent of the electorate backed Lukashenko's draft constitution on Sunday, allowing him to re-form parliament as two chambers, appoint half the constitutional court which opposes him and recommence his five-year term.
But his opponents said the vote was based on massive fraud and the outcome decreed in advance.
"It's a farce," said parliament speaker Semyon Sharetsky. "Belarus is heading for a real dictatorship."

Lukashenko said he would reorganise parliament into two chambers by the end of the year, though it was unclear exactly how. The president met deputies loyal to him on Monday but ignored Sharetsky and other parliamentary leaders.
Lukashenko says the deputies will approve the appointment of 110 of the existing 199 to a lower house and all but six of a 64-seat upper house.

Parliament is deeply divided between allies and foes of Lukashenko but the president insisted he would have no need to call new elections. "There will be consensus and harmony between president and parliament," he said.
There was also no mention by the central electoral commission, state television, or Lukashenko of the results of by-elections to 51 vacant seats in parliament.

Since winning the presidency by a landslide in July 1994, Lukashenko has become increasingly authoritarian, and the new constitution awards him powers over institutions which a Council of Europe analysis recently said "could not be stronger".

The population of 10 million voted amid a one-sided campaign from state television and radio, urging them to say "yes" to four questions proposed by the president and "no" to three tabled by parliament. Results showed Lukashenko winning all seven easily.

Viktor Gonchar, sacked by the president as the head of the electoral commission though he was appointed by parliament, told Reuters it was clear to him that the results had been faked since turnout was so high at more than 84 percent.
"Even during the presidential campaign (in 1994), when political activity was at its highest, it was lower. The figures are simply fantastic," he said.
Gonchar said the turnout in big towns had been particularly high during the last four hours of voting. "This would be understandable in summer, but not in late November," he said.
Parliament's draft constitution, which would have abolished the presidency and strengthened parliament, won the backing of just 7.9 percent of the electorate.
The electorate also voted overwhelmingly to keep the death penalty, let Lukashenko continue appointing local leaders and to keep a ban on the free sale and purchase of land.
"This election was decided before it began," the head of the International Helsinki Federation in Vienna, Aaron Rhodes, said by telephone.

Impeachment proceedings begun by deputies last week against the president are due to resume in the constitutional court on Tuesday but Lukashenko seemed confident the case would lapse. Parliament will also reconvene on Tuesday.

Asked what he would do if the court ruled against him, a move which would automatically transfer power to Sharetsky while parliament voted on the issue, Lukashenko cocked his head to one side and said: "You think they will?"
He made clear that the 11 court judges would have a chance of being reappointed, but only if they stopped trying to block his decisions.

He urged more than 70 deputies who signed last week's impeachment papers to to withdraw their signatures and said: "I think any resistance to the will of the people will, to put it mildly, be received negatively by the people".
Lukashenko, whose policies have led his country into isolation from international financial institutions, said he planned to carry out economic reforms.

The tall, moustached leader also told reporters he wanted Belarus to be part of the European Union -- a departure from his usual policy of looking only eastwards to Russia, with which he has formed a "community".
"Belarus is a European state and it must be in the family of European states," he said. Diplomats say that as things stand, Belarus has no chance of joining the EU.
